newsitem.title: INDIA: India heading for tenth successive normal monsoon.
newsitem.headline: India heading for tenth successive normal monsoon.

text.p: India's annual monsoon, crucial to farming and the health of the overall economy, is likely to yield a normal amount of rainfall for the tenth successive year in 1997, the Meteorological Department said on Sunday.
The department said in a statement that nine of 16 measures used to predict the monsoon were favourable and "there is a very good probability of a normal monsoon this year".
N. Sen Roy, director general of the Meteorological Department, told Reuters monsoon rainfall was expected to be about 92 percent of the long-term average, compared with 103 percent in 1996.
Analysts said the probability that rainfall would be slightly below average could hinder farm output.
"But then also it is too early to predict the impact of the monsoon on agricultural performance," Ashok Gulati, an economist at the National Council of Applied Economic Research, told Reuters.

The southwest monsoon rains usually strike the southwestern tip of the subcontinent around June 1, and move progressively north, eventually covering the entire country before tapering off in September.

"In 1997, the southwest monsoon rainfall over the country is likely to be normal,...thus making the year 1997 the 10th normal monsoon year in succession," the department said, adding that normal was defined as rainfall within 10 percent of average.
It said the monsoon rains were expected to hit the southern state of Kerala a few days after the normal arrival date of June 1.
"It will be definitely before June 10th," Roy told Reuters. "Even if the arrival is slightly delayed, it does not affect the overall performance of the monsoon."

In much of India, the southwest monsoon provides most of the annual rainfall. Agriculture employs about two thirds of India's workers and accounts for more than a quarter of its gross domestic product (GDP).
Adequate rainfall can bolster farm production, add to national income and keep prices down.

In the year ended March 31, the most evenly distributed rains in five years helped agricultural production to grow by 3.7 percent over the previous fiscal year. That underpinned overall GDP growth of 6.8 percent.
The Agriculture Ministry estimates foodgrains production in the 1996/97 season ending on June 30 to rise to 192.11 million tonnes from 185.04 million tonnes in the previous year.
Good rainfall can have significant ripple effects on the economy, including gold consumption. India is one of the biggest consumers of gold in the world.
A plentiful harvest increases disposable income in the hands of villagers, who then tend to buy more gold for annual Hindu festivals late in the calendar year.
